domain: OS and device integration web APIs: the native capability catalogue. Support was checked against MDN browser-compat-data 8.1.4 (2026-10-01; current releases Chrome 154, Safari 27, Firefox 157), MDN content, WebKit, Chrome and Firefox release notes. Every TS snippet was typechecked with TS 5.9 under strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes. TS 5.9's lib.dom is missing many of these APIs (MediaSession call actions, ScreenOrientation.lock, documentPictureInPicture, showOpenFilePicker, launchQueue, audioSession, BarcodeDetector, EyeDropper, SpeechRecognition, IdleDetector, NDEFReader, CloseWatcher, navigation, keyboard, contacts). The snippets declare the minimal shapes they use with `const w: Window & { api?: Shape } = window` and avoid lying casts.

items.title: User activation rules (transient vs sticky) and navigator.userActivation
items.what: Many native-feeling APIs only work during 'transient activation', a short window after a trusted keydown, mousedown, pointerdown (mouse), pointerup or touchend (touch/pen). Some APIs consume that activation. Others need only 'sticky' activation, meaning the user has interacted at least once. navigator.userActivation.isActive and .hasBeenActive expose both states.
items.why: Missing activation is the biggest single cause of 'the share sheet / copy / fullscreen button does nothing on iPhone'. If you design the tap flow around activation, every gated API works on the first tap, the way native buttons do.
items.support: Activation gating applies in every browser. navigator.userActivation: Chrome 72, Safari 16.4, Firefox 120. These need transient activation (MDN list): navigator.share, clipboard read/write, requestFullscreen, requestPictureInPicture, documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow, show*FilePicker, input.showPicker, PaymentRequest.show, window.open, getDisplayMedia, EyeDropper.open, contacts.select, requestStorageAccess, getScreenDetails, queryLocalFonts, Keyboard.lock, USB/HID/Serial request*, IdleDetector.requestPermission, Clients.openWindow, WindowClient.focus. These need sticky activation: navigator.vibrate, media/WebAudio autoplay, beforeunload prompts, VirtualKeyboard.show.
items.gotchas: On touch, pointerdown and touchstart do NOT grant activation; only pointerup and touchend do. A long-press timer that fires while the finger is still down has no activation, so copying or sharing from it fails. Run the action from the menu item's click instead. Safari is the strictest: any await (network, IndexedDB, crypto) before the gated call can lose activation. Prepare data before the tap, or use the Promise-in-ClipboardItem trick. window.open and some other APIs consume activation, so one tap cannot chain two consuming calls. Esc keydown does not grant activation. Automation clicks (Playwright) are trusted, so tests pass even when real taps would fail; test the order of awaits by reading the code.

items.title: Permission UX: ask in context after explaining, never on load (plus the new capability elements)
items.what: A pattern: show your own explainer UI where the feature lives, trigger the browser prompt only from the user's tap on it, and on denial show how to re-enable instead of re-prompting. Chrome now ships browser-drawn permission buttons, <geolocation> (Chrome 144) and <usermedia> (Chrome 151). They own the prompt and let users recover from an earlier 'Block'.
items.why: Native apps ask at the moment of need, with context. A web app that fires notification, location or camera prompts on load reads as spam. Chrome auto-quiets such sites and users block them for good.
items.support: The pattern is universal. Notification.requestPermission requires a user gesture in Firefox 72+ and in Safari; Chrome shows 'quiet' permission UI for sites with low accept rates. <geolocation>: Chrome/Edge 144 (desktop and Android). <usermedia>: Chrome/Edge 151. Safari and Firefox have neither and render the fallback children.
items.gotchas: Never chain several prompts (camera, mic, notifications) in one flow. Ask for the mic when joining a call, the camera when turning video on, notifications after the user's first conversation. On iOS a 'Don't Allow' is effectively permanent until the user changes Settings, so the explainer matters most there. Read the state with the Permissions API first and skip the card when it's already 'granted'. Capability elements impose styling limits: contrast at least 3:1, font size at least 'small', and opacity, line-height and so on clamped. At most 3 <geolocation> elements per page. Chrome cites big recovery gains (Cisco 10% to 65% permission recovery; Zoom 46.9% fewer capture errors). Yurt: Notification.requestPermission is only ever called from a user action.

items.title: Permissions API: query state and watch for changes
items.what: navigator.permissions.query({ name }) returns a PermissionStatus whose state is granted, denied or prompt, plus a 'change' event. Use it to decide which UI to show without triggering a prompt.
items.why: Native settings screens show live toggles. With this API, 'Notifications: On / Off / Blocked (how to fix)' stays accurate even when the user changes it in browser or OS settings.
items.support: query(): Chrome 43, Safari 16, Firefox 46; Android WebView has no Permissions API. Names: geolocation (all); notifications (Safari 16.4; in Firefox an alias of push); camera/microphone (Chrome 64, Safari 16, Firefox 132); screen-wake-lock (Chrome 84, Safari 16.4, Firefox 126); push (Safari 17); persistent-storage, storage-access; clipboard-read/clipboard-write, local-fonts, window-management, idle-detection, accelerometer and others are Chromium-only.
items.gotchas: Always wrap in try/catch, because an unsupported name throws TypeError instead of returning 'prompt'. 'prompt' means you may ask (after explaining). 'denied' means show per-browser steps to re-enable and never loop prompts. Yurt lesson: Notification.permission can lag behind the browser's settings, so read notification permission live via permissions.query. In an iOS Safari tab, 'Notification' is undefined; check that before querying. Some browsers return 'prompt' for camera/mic even after a one-time 'Allow this time'.

items.title: Web Share API (navigator.share / canShare), including files
items.what: Opens the OS share sheet with title, text, url and (Level 2) files. Resolves when the user shares. Rejects with AbortError when they dismiss it.
items.why: The system share sheet (AirDrop, Messages, WhatsApp, Nearby Share) replaces home-made 'copy link / tweet this' rows, one of the most obvious web tells on phones.
items.support: Safari 12.1 macOS / iOS 12.2 (files from 14). Chrome Android 61 (files 76). Chrome desktop: Windows/ChromeOS since 89, all of Windows/ChromeOS/macOS since 128, not Linux. Edge Windows 81+. Firefox Android 79 (no files). Firefox desktop only behind a flag. Android WebView: no. Secure context only; iframes need allow="web-share".
items.gotchas: Yurt lessons: AbortError (user cancelled) is silent and anything else gets a toast. Never press Share in headless tests: navigator.share brought headless Chromium down on macOS. Test the fallback and the error mapping instead. Needs transient activation, which share consumes, so don't await anything before it. A double tap while the sheet is open gives InvalidStateError. Many targets ignore 'title'. When both text and url are given, some targets concatenate or drop one, so put the link in 'url' only. canShare({files}) returns false for disallowed file types: check it before offering 'Share image'. On desktop Chrome the sheet is small and OS-dependent; offer 'Copy link' alongside it.

items.title: Web Share Target (manifest share_target, including files)
items.what: Lets an installed PWA appear as a destination in the OS share sheet. The manifest declares an action URL and parameter names. Files arrive as a multipart POST that the service worker handles.
items.why: Being a share target ('Share to <YourApp>' from Photos or the browser) is what makes an installed app feel like a peer of native apps instead of a bookmark.
items.support: Chrome/Edge Android (76+) for installed apps, plus Samsung Internet. ChromeOS desktop (Chrome 89; desktop Windows/macOS share sheets don't reliably list PWAs, so verify per OS). Safari: no. Firefox Android parses the field with no effect.
items.gotchas: Only installed apps appear. A manifest change takes effect after the app updates or reinstalls. Android usually puts shared URLs in 'text', not 'url', so extract URLs from text. Treat every field and file as untrusted input (validate the type and size). The action must be inside the manifest scope and handled by the SW even when offline. If the app is cold-starting, the page has to collect the stashed files (cache/IDB) after the redirect. Combine with launch_handler so the share opens in the existing window.

items.title: Badging API (setAppBadge / clearAppBadge)
items.what: Sets a number or dot on the installed app's icon (dock, taskbar, home screen). It also works from the service worker, so the badge updates while the app is closed.
items.why: Unread counts on the icon are a core native-messaging signal. Without them an installed web app looks dead next to Slack or WhatsApp.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 81 desktop on Windows and macOS (ChromeOS 91). Linux has no OS badge. Chrome Android: no numeric badge; launcher dots come from notifications (clearAppBadge exists). Safari iOS/iPadOS 16.4+ for Home Screen web apps. Safari macOS 17+ (Sonoma) for Dock web apps. Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: On iOS the badge only appears once notification permission is granted; badging rides on that permission. In iOS 26 any site added to the Home Screen opens as a web app by default, so more users have one. Yurt lesson: in a browser tab the call rejects or does nothing; swallow it and don't toast. setAppBadge() with no argument shows a dot. On Safari setAppBadge(0) clears it. Clear it when the user reads (also from the SW on notificationclick). Don't badge non-actionable counts.

items.title: Notifications via the service worker (+ actions, tag, click routing)
items.what: Show system notifications with ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification (title, body, icon, badge, tag, data, actions), handle notificationclick in the SW, and focus or route the existing window.
items.why: System notifications that open straight to the right conversation, don't open a second window, and collapse per thread feel native. Duplicates, page reloads and stale notifications feel webby.
items.support: Chrome desktop/Android; on Android `new Notification()` throws, so use the SW only. Firefox 22+; actions and maxActions since Firefox 152. Safari macOS 16+ (Ventura). iOS/iPadOS 16.4+ only in Home Screen web apps, where Notification is undefined in a tab. Actions: Chrome/Edge and Firefox 152, not Safari. tag replacement: not Safari (settable, no effect). renotify, image: Chromium only. silent: Chrome, Firefox 132, Safari 16.6 macOS. requireInteraction: Chromium (Firefox Windows only). Safari 18.4 adds Declarative Web Push (window.pushManager plus a JSON payload the OS displays without running SW code).
items.gotchas: Yurt lessons: ask only from a user action. In a Safari tab the SW registers without showNotification/getNotifications, and calling getNotifications there threw, so feature-detect on the registration (notifiesThroughWorker). Validate notification.data (it's unknown). If a window is open, postMessage plus focus() instead of openWindow (no reload). Don't notify for the conversation the user is looking at (check focus and visibility). The badge icon should be a monochrome alpha mask for Android's status bar. Pushes must always show a notification (userVisibleOnly) or Safari and Chrome revoke push. Notification copy shows on the lock screen: keep secrets out of it in E2E-encrypted apps.

items.title: Page Visibility and lifecycle (visibilitychange, pagehide, pageshow/bfcache)
items.what: document.visibilityState and the visibilitychange event tell you when the app goes to the background or app switcher. pagehide and pageshow (with e.persisted) cover navigation and back/forward-cache restores.
items.why: Native apps save drafts, pause work, mark you 'away' when backgrounded and refresh instantly when foregrounded. Web apps that lose drafts or show stale data on return feel broken.
items.support: Universal (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, desktop and mobile). Safari 14.1+ fires visibilitychange reliably when the user navigates away or switches apps. freeze/resume (Page Lifecycle) events are Chromium-only.
items.gotchas: After 'hidden' the OS may kill the page without another event, so persist there (IndexedDB writes may not finish; keep them small). Timers are throttled or frozen in the background, so recompute from Date.now() on return instead of trusting setInterval counts. A desktop window behind other windows is still 'visible'; use document.hasFocus() for that. Yurt lesson: headless test browsers always report a visible page and faking document.hidden tests the fake, so keep the hidden branch to one line. Don't use beforeunload except for real unsaved changes.

items.title: Web Locks + BroadcastChannel for multi-tab coordination (leader election)
items.what: navigator.locks.request(name, cb) is an origin-wide async mutex that is released when the callback settles or the tab dies. BroadcastChannel sends messages between same-origin tabs, windows and workers. Together they elect one 'leader' tab that owns the socket, sync or notifications.
items.why: Native apps are single-instance. Without coordination, three open tabs make three sockets, three notification copies and racing IndexedDB writes. With a leader, every tab behaves like one app.
items.support: Web Locks: Chrome 69, Safari 15.4, Firefox 96. BroadcastChannel: Chrome 54, Safari 15.4, Firefox 38. Both work in workers.
items.gotchas: BroadcastChannel never delivers to the sending context, so the leader must handle its own events. Messages can come from an older or newer app version in another tab: validate and version them. Use { ifAvailable: true } for 'try-lock' and { steal: true } only for recovery. Locks are per origin (and storage partition): an installed app window and a browser tab of the same origin share them. Holding a lock forever is the intended pattern for leadership; to give it up, resolve the promise via an AbortSignal (signal option). Pages holding locks may be ineligible for bfcache in some browsers (not verified per browser).

items.title: Async Clipboard API (text, rich text, images, ClipboardItem) + paste event
items.what: navigator.clipboard.writeText/write/readText/read with ClipboardItem for multiple MIME types. ClipboardItem.supports(type) checks support. Paste uses the plain 'paste' event and clipboardData.files.
items.why: One-tap 'Copy link' with a confirmation, copying images out, and pasting screenshots straight into the composer are all native-app staples.
items.support: writeText: Chrome 66, Safari 13.1/iOS 13.4, Firefox 63. write + ClipboardItem: Chrome 76 (Android 84), Safari 13.1, Firefox 127. ClipboardItem.supports: Chrome 121, Safari 18.4, Firefox 127. readText/read: Chrome (clipboard-read permission prompt), Safari (shows a system 'Paste' callout the user must tap), Firefox 125/127 (paste prompt unless the content is same-origin). The clipboardchange event: Chrome 144 only.
items.gotchas: Writes need transient activation in Safari and Firefox (always), and in Chrome since 107 unless clipboard-write is granted. Chrome and Firefox accept only ONE ClipboardItem per write. Only image/png is reliably writable. 'Document is not focused' (NotAllowedError) happens when DevTools or another frame has focus. Avoid read(): the Safari/Firefox paste callouts feel alien; use the paste event or Ctrl/Cmd+V. Yurt lessons: a refused clipboard is reported with a toast, not swallowed; the composer takes pasted files from clipboardData.files. Permission names clipboard-read/clipboard-write exist only in Chromium. Copying from a touch long-press timer fails (no activation yet).

items.title: <input type=file accept capture> for camera, photos and files on phones
items.what: A plain file input gives the native picker: on iOS a sheet with Photo Library / Take Photo / Choose File, on Android camera plus files. accept filters types. capture="environment" or capture="user" opens the camera directly.
items.why: The native photo picker and camera beat any custom getUserMedia camera UI for 'attach a photo'. They're fast, familiar, need no camera permission prompt, and give full-resolution images.
items.how:
<!-- Let the user choose: library, camera or files -->
<label class="attach"><input type="file" accept="image/*,video/*" multiple hidden data-testid="attach">Attach</label>
<!-- 'Scan document' / 'Take photo': straight to the rear camera (phones only; desktops ignore capture) -->
<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="environment">
<!-- Selfie -->
<input type="file" accept="image/*" capture="user">
// TS
input.addEventListener('change', () => attach([...(input.files ?? [])]));
input.addEventListener('cancel', () => {/* picker dismissed: Chrome 113, Safari 16.4, Firefox 91 */});
items.support: accept and multiple: universal. capture: Chrome Android 25, iOS Safari 10, Firefox Android 79, Android WebView; desktop browsers ignore it. webkitdirectory (folder pick): desktop browsers, iOS 18.4+, Chrome Android 132+.
items.gotchas: capture removes the library and files options, so use it only for explicit 'take photo' buttons. iOS usually transcodes HEIC to JPEG on upload, but don't rely on it: check file.type and convert if needed. Camera photos are huge: downscale with createImageBitmap plus (Offscreen)Canvas before upload, and strip EXIF GPS for privacy. Opening the picker may background the page or fire blur/visibilitychange on mobile, so don't treat that as the user leaving. Clicking a hidden input programmatically must happen inside the user's tap. The input's change event doesn't fire on cancel; listen to 'cancel'.

items.title: Drag and drop files (in) with folder support
items.what: dragover/dragleave/drop on a drop zone using DataTransfer.types, files and items. webkitGetAsEntry() walks folders. Chromium also offers getAsFileSystemHandle().
items.why: Dragging files from Finder or Explorer onto a conversation or document is basic desktop-app behavior. A browser that navigates to file:// when you miss the zone is a jarring web tell.
items.support: Desktop: universal. iPadOS Safari accepts drops from Files and Photos. Phones: very limited. webkitGetAsEntry: Chrome 13, Safari 11.1, Firefox 50 (Android 141). DataTransferItem.getAsFileSystemHandle (writable handles): Chromium 86 desktop, Chrome Android 132.
items.gotchas: Yurt lessons: only react when types includes 'Files', and clear the 'dragging' state only when the event target is the zone itself (React's onDragLeave flickers over children). During dragover, files is empty (protected mode); only types is readable. Call webkitGetAsEntry/getAsFileSystemHandle synchronously in the drop handler. Dragging files OUT of the app to the desktop needs the Chromium-only 'DownloadURL' data type. Give a visible drop overlay with a clear label.

items.title: File System Access (showOpenFilePicker / showSaveFilePicker) with fallbacks; OPFS
items.what: Native open and save dialogs that return file handles you can write back to ('Save' instead of 'Download copy'). The fallback is <input type=file> plus <a download>. The Origin Private File System (navigator.storage.getDirectory) is fast private storage available everywhere.
items.why: Real Save/Save As to the same file, recent-files lists and no 'file(3).json' download spam make a web editor feel like a desktop app.
items.support: showOpenFilePicker/showSaveFilePicker/showDirectoryPicker: Chrome/Edge desktop 86, Chrome Android 132. Safari and Firefox: none. OPFS getDirectory: Chrome 86, Safari 15.2, Firefox 111. FileSystemFileHandle.createWritable: Chrome 86, Firefox 111, Safari 26.
items.gotchas: Cancel throws AbortError: treat it as a no-op. Needs transient activation. Handles stored in IndexedDB survive reloads but need handle.queryPermission/requestPermission({ mode: 'readwrite' }) again (Chromium only). The library 'browser-fs-access' wraps both paths. Safari's download fallback saves to Downloads with no dialog. OPFS is not user-visible and can be evicted unless navigator.storage.persist() is granted.

items.title: Passkeys / WebAuthn: conditional mediation (autofill), getClientCapabilities, automatic upgrade
items.what: Use passkeys for sign-in through the OS credential manager (Face ID, Touch ID, Windows Hello, Google Password Manager). Conditional mediation shows passkeys in the username field's autofill. Conditional create silently adds a passkey right after a password sign-in. getClientCapabilities() detects all of this.
items.why: Biometric one-tap sign-in in the keyboard autofill bar is exactly how native apps sign in. Password-plus-SMS forms are a web tell.
items.how:
<input name="username" autocomplete="username webauthn" autofocus>
<input name="password" type="password" autocomplete="current-password">
// TS: validate server JSON with your schema lib before trusting its shape
declare const loginOptions: () => Promise<PublicKeyCredentialRequestOptionsJSON>, registerOptions: () => Promise<PublicKeyCredentialCreationOptionsJSON>, fetchJson: (url: string, body?: unknown) => Promise<unknown>;
let autofill = new AbortController();
export async function passkeyAutofill() { // on load of the sign-in screen
  const caps = (await PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities?.()) ?? {};
  if (!caps['conditionalGet']) return;
  const publicKey = PublicKeyCredential.parseRequestOptionsFromJSON(await loginOptions());
  try {
    const cred = await navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey, mediation: 'conditional', signal: autofill.signal });
    if (cred instanceof PublicKeyCredential) await fetchJson('/webauthn/login', cred.toJSON());
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof DOMException && (e.name === 'NotAllowedError' || e.name === 'AbortError')) return; // cancelled
    throw e;
  }
}
export async function passkeyButton() { // explicit button: abort the pending autofill first
  autofill.abort(); autofill = new AbortController();
  const publicKey = PublicKeyCredential.parseRequestOptionsFromJSON(await loginOptions());
  const cred = await navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey, signal: autofill.signal });
  if (cred instanceof PublicKeyCredential) await fetchJson('/webauthn/login', cred.toJSON());
}
export async function upgradeToPasskey() { // right after a successful password sign-in
  const caps = (await PublicKeyCredential.getClientCapabilities?.()) ?? {};
  if (!caps['conditionalCreate']) return;
  const publicKey = PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON(await registerOptions());
  const options: CredentialCreationOptions & { mediation: 'conditional' } = { publicKey, mediation: 'conditional' }; // TS lib lacks it
  const cred = await navigator.credentials.create(options).catch(() => null);
  if (cred instanceof PublicKeyCredential) await fetchJson('/webauthn/register', cred.toJSON());
}
items.support: WebAuthn: all modern browsers. Conditional get: Chrome 108, Safari 16, Firefox 119 (Android WebView always reports false). getClientCapabilities: Chrome 133, Safari 17.4, Firefox 135. parse*OptionsFromJSON: Chrome 129, Safari 18.4, Firefox 119. signalUnknownCredential: Chrome 132, Safari 26. Conditional create (automatic upgrade): Safari 18 (iOS 18/macOS 15), Chrome 136 desktop, Chrome Android 142 per Chrome's docs.
items.gotchas: Start conditional get on page load and keep it pending; the 'webauthn' token must be the last autocomplete token. Abort it before a modal passkey call or the calls collide. NotAllowedError means the user cancelled or timed out, so stay silent. The rpId is the registrable domain: apps on a shared host (e.g. *.github.io project pages) should move to a custom domain before shipping passkeys. When the server says a credential is unknown (404), call PublicKeyCredential.signalUnknownCredential({ rpId, credentialId: json.id }) so the OS manager deletes it. The provider may silently decline conditional create, and Chrome only allows it shortly (about 5 minutes) after a password-manager sign-in. Use the base64url id, not rawId.

items.title: One-time codes: autocomplete="one-time-code" (iOS/macOS) + WebOTP (Android)
items.what: Mark the code field with autocomplete="one-time-code". With a domain-bound SMS format, iOS and macOS offer the code from Messages (and Mail) above the keyboard, and Android Chrome's WebOTP API reads it with user consent.
items.why: 'From Messages: 123456' above the keyboard is the native sign-in experience. Making users switch apps and retype the code is a web tell.
items.how:
<input name="otp" autocomplete="one-time-code" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{6}" maxlength="6">
<!-- SMS body, last line binds it to your origin (both platforms):
Your code is 123456

@app.example.com #123456 -->
// TS (Android WebOTP; harmless elsewhere)
if ('OTPCredential' in window) {
  const ac = new AbortController();
  form.addEventListener('submit', () => ac.abort(), { once: true });
  const options: CredentialRequestOptions & { otp: { transport: ['sms'] } } = { otp: { transport: ['sms'] }, signal: ac.signal };
  navigator.credentials.get(options).then(
    (c) => { if (c && 'code' in c && typeof c.code === 'string') { input.value = c.code; form.requestSubmit(); } },
    () => {}, // aborted or declined: the user types it
  );
}
items.support: autocomplete=one-time-code: Safari iOS 12+/macOS (domain-bound codes iOS 14+), and Chrome/Android autofill. WebOTP (OTPCredential): Chrome Android 84; Chrome desktop 93 (cross-device from a signed-in Android phone). No WebOTP in Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: Use a single real input. Six separate boxes break autofill (or make the first box receive the paste and distribute it). Use inputmode=numeric, not type=number (that strips leading zeros and adds spinners). WebOTP shows a consent sheet and only matches the exact origin in the @domain line; for iframes use '@top.example #code @embedded.example'. Don't auto-submit before the user can see the code if it might be wrong; do clear and refocus on error. Prefer passkeys and use OTP as the fallback.

items.title: Media Session API (lock-screen and notification controls, artwork, position, call mute and hang-up)
items.what: navigator.mediaSession.metadata (title, artist, artwork), setActionHandler (play, pause, seekto, next/previoustrack, and for calls togglemicrophone, togglecamera, hangup), setPositionState for the scrubber, and setMicrophoneActive/setCameraActive to report call state to the OS or browser.
items.why: Lock-screen, Control Center, notification-shade and keyboard media-key controls with artwork are what make audio/video feel native. Without them the OS shows 'example.com' and the buttons don't work. For calls, the browser's PiP window and OS mute indicators stay in sync.
items.support: MediaSession: Chrome 73 desktop / 57 Android, Safari 15 (macOS, iOS), Firefox 82 (Firefox Android exposes it but shows no UI). Android WebView: no. setMicrophoneActive/setCameraActive and togglemicrophone/togglecamera: Chrome 93, Safari 18.4. hangup: Chrome 93 only. setScreenshareActive: Safari 18.4 only. enterpictureinpicture action (lets Chrome auto-open PiP when the user switches tabs): Chrome 120.
items.gotchas: Lock-screen controls appear only while a real <audio>/<video> element is playing; WebAudio-only playback often gets no controls, so route through a media element. setPositionState throws on NaN or Infinity duration (live streams), so guard it. Registering seekbackward/seekforward changes which buttons iOS shows (skip ±10s instead of prev/next). Artwork should be same-origin or CORS-enabled, in several sizes. For calls, call setMicrophoneActive after every mute change so the OS indicator matches; Safari 18.4 fixed repeated mic prompts. Clear handlers (setAction(x, null)) and metadata when playback or the call ends, otherwise stale controls linger.

items.title: Audio Session API (navigator.audioSession.type): mix, duck or own the audio
items.what: A page-wide hint for how the app's audio interacts with other apps' audio and the device: auto, playback, transient, transient-solo, ambient or play-and-record.
items.why: The default ('auto' → 'playback' for media) makes a 'message received' pop STOP the user's music or podcast on iPhone, a very un-native behavior. 'ambient' mixes like native UI sounds do. 'play-and-record' gives proper call routing.
items.support: navigator.audioSession.type: Safari 16.4+ macOS and iOS according to MDN BCD (widely described as shipping for real use in iOS 17). AudioSession.state and statechange (active/interrupted/inactive): Firefox Nightly only per BCD. Chrome and Firefox stable: none (feature-detect and no-op).
items.gotchas: It's one global per page, so switch it around the activity (call vs podcast vs UI sounds) and restore it afterwards. 'playback' interrupts other apps and plays through the silent switch on iPhone. 'ambient' mixes and, as an iOS ambient category, is expected to respect the silent switch (verify on device). 'transient' ducks other audio for short prompts. WebKit infers play-and-record while getUserMedia is active, but set it explicitly before capture to avoid route glitches (earpiece vs speaker, Bluetooth). A ringtone the user must hear might need 'playback' or 'transient'; test with music playing and the silent switch on.

items.title: Unlock sound in the first gesture (autoplay policy)
items.what: Browsers only allow audible playback after user activation, and iOS needs that same media element (or AudioContext) to have been started inside a gesture. Prime the ringtone or notification element muted in the first tap, then play it later without a gesture.
items.why: Incoming-call rings and message sounds that just work, like native, instead of failing silently until the user happens to tap.
items.support: All browsers enforce an autoplay policy (Chrome's Media Engagement Index can relax it for frequently used sites and installed apps). iOS is the strictest: reuse the primed element.
items.gotchas: Yurt lesson (ringer): a call before any tap still shows on screen, it just can't sound, so design the visual ring to stand alone. Listen on pointerdown (mouse activation) AND pointerup/keydown (touch and keyboard activation). Reuse one element; creating new Audio() per sound needs a new gesture on iOS. Pair with audioSession 'ambient' for UI sounds. Respect a 'sounds off' setting and the OS silent mode where you can.

items.title: Screen Wake Lock (and re-acquire on visibilitychange)
items.what: navigator.wakeLock.request('screen') keeps the display from dimming or locking. The browser releases the lock whenever the page is hidden, so you must request it again when the page becomes visible.
items.why: Calls, recipes, slides, boarding passes and QR codes on screen shouldn't go dark mid-use. Native apps hold the screen on; the old web hacks (looping invisible video) are obsolete.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 84 (desktop and Android), Safari 16.4 (macOS and iOS tabs), Firefox 126. iOS Home Screen web apps: broken from 16.4 to 18.3 (WebKit bug 254545), fixed in iOS 18.4. Android WebView 84.
items.gotchas: Only hold it while the activity is on screen (in a call, in cooking mode) and release it after. Requests fail when the page is hidden, and can fail under battery saver or policy, so never surface the error loudly. Iframes need Permissions-Policy: screen-wake-lock. Don't request it on load just because; it drains battery. There is no system wake lock (keeping the CPU awake) on the web.

items.title: Picture-in-Picture for video (incl. WebRTC call video)
items.what: video.requestPictureInPicture() floats a <video> (including a MediaStream from a call) in an always-on-top OS window. Safari also has the legacy webkitSetPresentationMode('picture-in-picture').
items.why: Keep watching, or keep seeing the other person in a call, while using other apps, as native video and FaceTime do.
items.support: Chrome 69 desktop / Chrome Android 105. Safari 13.1 macOS / iOS 13.4 per BCD (iPhone PiP since iOS 14). Firefox 153 desktop has the JS API (its built-in PiP toggle existed before). Firefox Android: no. Android WebView: no. Chrome 120+: a mediaSession 'enterpictureinpicture' handler enables automatic PiP on tab switch for eligible sites.
items.gotchas: Needs user activation (except automatic PiP) and loaded metadata (readyState ≥ 1). Only <video> works; for arbitrary UI use Document PiP. Put the media session hangup/togglemicrophone handlers in place so Chrome's PiP window shows call controls. Respect disablepictureinpicture on decorative videos. iOS auto-PiP on home-swipe works for playing inline videos with playsinline.

items.title: Document Picture-in-Picture (always-on-top window with arbitrary HTML)
items.what: documentPictureInPicture.requestWindow() opens an always-on-top mini window that you fill with your own DOM: call controls, a timer, a mini chat, a now-playing card.
items.why: Mini players and floating call windows with real buttons (mute, hang up, raise hand) are native desktop conventions that video-only PiP can't do.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 116 desktop; Firefox 151 desktop (May 2026). Safari: no. Mobile: no.
items.gotchas: Needs user activation; one PiP window per page. The stylesheet copy is one-time, so theme changes or later-injected CSS (CSS-in-JS) need re-copying or a MutationObserver. Copy color-scheme and data-theme attributes too. In React, render into pip.document.body with a portal instead of moving framework-owned nodes. The window can't navigate and closes when the opener navigates or closes. disallowReturnToOpener hides the 'back to tab' button. Size hints get clamped.

items.title: Fullscreen API (and the iPhone limits)
items.what: element.requestFullscreen({ navigationUI }) hides browser UI for an element. :fullscreen and ::backdrop let you style it. On iPhone only a <video> can go fullscreen, via the non-standard webkitEnterFullscreen() (native player).
items.why: Immersive viewers (photos, slides, games, video) without browser chrome feel like native full-screen views.
items.support: Chrome 71 (prefixed earlier), Firefox 64, Safari 16.4 unprefixed on macOS (webkit-prefixed since 5.1). iPadOS: element fullscreen (16.4 unprefixed) with a forced overlay exit button, and swiping down exits. iPhone: no element fullscreen, only <video>.webkitEnterFullscreen().
items.gotchas: Needs user activation. Esc, back or swipe exits, so keep your state in sync via fullscreenchange. On iPhone the 'fullscreen' experience is an installed web app with display: standalone (or fullscreen), so ask users to install for games and kiosks. navigationUI: 'hide' is honored by Chrome Android. Fullscreen is a prerequisite for Keyboard Lock and Screen Orientation lock. Don't use it for ordinary app screens.

items.title: Screen Orientation: read always, lock only in fullscreen or installed apps
items.what: screen.orientation.type/angle plus a 'change' event everywhere. screen.orientation.lock('landscape') only where the platform allows it (Android in fullscreen, recent Firefox). Installed apps can declare the manifest 'orientation' field.
items.why: Games and video players that rotate and stay landscape feel native. Locking an ordinary app is anti-native on tablets, foldables and desktops.
items.support: lock(): Chrome Android 38 (fullscreen; Chrome also allows installed-app windows, so verify on target devices). Firefox Android and desktop 144+. Chrome/Edge desktop always throws NotSupportedError. Safari/iOS: no lock (screen.orientation is readable since 16.4). The manifest orientation field is honored by Android installed apps.
items.gotchas: iOS can't lock. For games, show a 'rotate your device' overlay with @media (orientation: portrait) instead. lock() rejects with SecurityError when the page is hidden and AbortError if superseded. Call unlock() on exit. Use CSS orientation and aspect-ratio media queries plus container queries for layout rather than locking.

items.title: Camera via getUserMedia: facingMode, playsinline, mirroring, torch; <usermedia> element
items.what: getUserMedia({ video: { facingMode } }) for live camera UIs (scanning, video calls, AR). Track capabilities and constraints add torch and zoom. Chrome 151's <usermedia> element is a browser-drawn camera/mic button that owns the prompt and returns the MediaStream.
items.why: A live preview that starts on the right camera, mirrors the selfie view and doesn't jump to fullscreen on iPhone feels like the native camera.
items.support: getUserMedia: all modern browsers (secure context). facingMode: mobile browsers. torch: Chrome Android. ImageCapture (full-res takePhoto): Chrome 59, Safari 18.4. getCapabilities: Chrome 59, Safari 11, Firefox 132. <usermedia>: Chrome/Edge 151 (desktop and Android); others render the fallback children.
items.gotchas: Without playsinline and muted, iOS opens the video fullscreen and blocks autoplay. Use { ideal } constraints, not { exact } (exact throws OverconstrainedError on desktops). enumerateDevices() labels are empty until permission is granted; listen to devicechange for headsets and cameras plugged in. Stop tracks when leaving the screen. Yurt: request the mic only when joining a huddle, the camera only when turning video on; no media tests in E2E (accepted gap). <usermedia> API caveat: Chrome's blog documents a 'stream' event and a .stream property; the WICG explainer also mentions 'streamready'. Verify against Chrome's current docs before relying on the event name.

items.title: Geolocation (+ the <geolocation> element)
items.what: navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition/watchPosition, now optionally fronted by Chrome's <geolocation> element: a browser-drawn 'Use location' button that handles the prompt and fires 'location' events.
items.why: A clear 'Use my location' action at the moment of need, with fast low-accuracy results, mirrors native apps. Prompting for location on load is a top web annoyance.
items.support: Geolocation API: universal (secure context only). <geolocation> element: Chrome/Edge 144 (desktop and Android); Safari and Firefox render the fallback content. The element supports autolocate and watch attributes.
items.gotchas: Ask only on an explicit action. enableHighAccuracy: true wakes GPS (slow, battery), so start coarse. watchPosition effectively stops in background tabs on mobile, so the web can't do background location. On iOS, Settings > Privacy > Location Services > Safari Websites must be on; explain that when the error is PERMISSION_DENIED. The element enforces styling rules (contrast, size; at most 3 per page) and has isValid/invalidReason for clickjacking blockers.

items.title: DeviceOrientation/DeviceMotion (+ requestPermission) and Generic Sensor APIs
items.what: deviceorientation and devicemotion events for tilt, compass and shake, gated on iOS (and now in Chromium) by DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission() from a tap. The Chromium-only Generic Sensor classes (Accelerometer, Gyroscope, AbsoluteOrientationSensor…) offer frequency control.
items.why: Tilt parallax, compass headings, shake-to-undo and level tools feel physical and native when they work on iOS too.
items.support: Events: mobile browsers broadly; desktop only with sensors. requestPermission: iOS Safari (since iOS 13; MDN BCD lists 14.5). Chromium added it in 2026 (ChromeStatus: 151; MDN BCD: 152). Firefox: no requestPermission. Generic Sensors: Chrome 67+ (Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Linear/GravitySensor, Absolute/RelativeOrientationSensor); Magnetometer and AmbientLightSensor only behind flags; no Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: Code that treated 'requestPermission exists' as 'this is iOS' and only attached listeners on the iOS path broke on Chrome 152, so always attach after the check. iOS keeps a denial until site data is reset. Iframes need Permissions-Policy (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer). Use webkitCompassHeading on iOS for a true compass. Throttle work via requestAnimationFrame. Respect prefers-reduced-motion for parallax. Don't use AmbientLightSensor for theming; use prefers-color-scheme.

items.title: CloseWatcher and <dialog closedby>: Android back and Esc close your overlays
items.what: CloseWatcher turns the platform 'close request' (Android back button or gesture, Esc, assistive-tech dismiss) into a close event for custom sheets, drawers and menus. Modal <dialog> (showModal) and popover=auto already join the same close stack; closedby="any" adds light dismiss.
items.why: On Android, back must close the open sheet, not leave the app. That's the most common 'this is a website' moment for Android users.
items.support: CloseWatcher: Chrome/Edge 126 (desktop and Android), Firefox 149, Safari Technology Preview (enabled by default in WebKit trunk, not in Safari 27.0). <dialog closedby>: Chrome 134, Firefox 141, Safari TP. Modal dialog and popover=auto Esc handling: all browsers (popover light-dismiss on iOS fixed in 18.3).
items.gotchas: Without CloseWatcher, the old fallback (history.pushState per overlay plus popstate) is fragile; the Navigation API or just Esc support is the pragmatic fallback. Several watchers created without user activation get grouped, so one back press closes all of them (anti-abuse). oncancel with preventDefault (for 'discard changes?') only works with activation. Destroy the watcher when the UI closes by other means. Always keep a visible close button for iOS, which has no back gesture for in-page overlays.

items.title: Navigation API: one router hook for links, back/forward and form posts
items.what: window.navigation's 'navigate' event lets an SPA intercept every same-document navigation (link clicks, back and forward gestures, form submissions) with e.intercept({ handler }). It knows the navigation type and direction.
items.why: Correct back and forward behavior, direction-aware push/pop transitions and no full reloads are how native navigation stacks behave. It replaces brittle History API plus click-hijacking routers.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 102, Firefox 147 (Jan 2026), Safari 26.2 (Dec 2025), so it's newly Baseline. Older Safari and Firefox need a History API fallback.
items.gotchas: Feature-detect and keep a fallback router for iOS < 26.2. Intercepted handlers get e.signal, which aborts when another navigation supersedes them; pass it to fetch. Don't intercept downloads, cross-origin or hash-only navigations. Use navigation.back() and navigation.entries() for 'back to list' behavior instead of guessing with history.length. Scroll restoration and focus handling come built in after the handler resolves.

items.title: Haptics: navigator.vibrate (Android) with reduced-motion and a user setting
items.what: navigator.vibrate(pattern) gives short tactile feedback on Android browsers. iOS has no Vibration API.
items.why: Subtle taps on send, on a long-press threshold or on a mention make touch UIs feel physical and native.
items.support: Chrome Android 32 (needs sticky activation since Chrome 60; not in cross-origin iframes), Android WebView. Firefox: removed on desktop in 129, disabled on Android (returns true, no vibration). Safari/iOS: none. Safari 17.4+ has a native <input type=checkbox switch> that gives the system haptic when toggled on iOS 18.
items.gotchas: Yurt lessons: patterns of 8 ms (tap), 14 ms (tick) and [12, 60, 12] (notice) feel like UI, not alerts; gate on a user setting and prefers-reduced-motion. Requires sticky activation, so calls before the first tap are ignored. Community hacks programmatically click a hidden switch's <label> to trigger iOS haptics. That is undocumented and may break in any iOS update (unverified), so don't depend on it. Never use vibration as the only signal.

items.title: Network status: online/offline events, Network Information (Chromium), Battery Status (don't)
items.what: online/offline events and navigator.onLine everywhere. Chromium's navigator.connection (effectiveType, saveData, downlink, rtt) as an adaptive hint. The Battery Status API exists only in Chromium; avoid it.
items.why: An honest offline banner and queued sends, like native messengers, plus lighter media on Save-Data, instead of spinners that never resolve.
items.support: online/offline and navigator.onLine: universal. NetworkInformation: Chrome 61 desktop / 38 Android; saveData Chrome 65. Safari: none. Firefox: removed. Battery Status (navigator.getBattery): Chromium only, removed from Firefox 52 over fingerprinting, never in Safari.
items.gotchas: Don't block features on effectiveType; it's a coarse estimate. The server can read the Save-Data request header. Base connection UI on your transport's real state (WebSocket and relay health) with backoff, and use online/offline as a nudge to retry right away. Don't build features on battery level; if you must save power, use Compute Pressure, Page Visibility and the user's settings.

items.title: Launch Handler (single-instance app windows) + launchQueue
items.what: The manifest launch_handler.client_mode (auto, focus-existing, navigate-existing, navigate-new; an array is a fallback list) controls whether opening the installed app from a link, notification, share or file reuses the existing window. launchQueue.setConsumer delivers the target URL.
items.why: Native apps are single-instance: clicking a link or notification focuses the open app instead of spawning a second window.
items.support: launch_handler: Chrome/Edge 110 (desktop, and Android per BCD). launchQueue: Chromium 102 desktop. Safari and Firefox: no (they keep their default behavior).
items.gotchas: With focus-existing the page is NOT navigated; you must route to targetURL yourself, otherwise the user sees the old screen. navigate-existing reloads the existing window (state is lost). Combine with notificationclick → client.focus() and postMessage for in-app routing on every browser. It only applies to installed apps.

items.title: File Handling (manifest file_handlers + launchQueue files)
items.what: Registers the installed PWA as an OS handler for file types (shown in 'Open with', or as the default app). The opened files arrive as FileSystemFileHandles through launchQueue, so the app can save back to them.
items.why: Double-clicking a .md or .csv to open it in your app, and saving back to the same file, is the definition of a desktop app.
items.support: Chromium desktop 102 (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS) for installed apps. Android, Safari and Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: The OS asks the user the first time a file type opens with your app. Only installed apps qualify. Declare specific types (no */*). Writing back may prompt for write permission. Keep an <input type=file> path for everyone else.

items.title: Protocol handlers (registerProtocolHandler / manifest protocol_handlers)
items.what: Lets the app handle custom schemes (web+yourapp:) or safelisted ones (mailto:, tel:, magnet:, webcal:, xmpp:, matrix:…), so clicking such links anywhere opens your app.
items.why: Deep links like 'mailto:' opening your mail app or 'web+chat:' opening your chat are how native apps integrate with the OS.
items.support: registerProtocolHandler: Chrome/Edge desktop, Firefox desktop (Firefox Android 4+ per BCD). Safari: no. Chrome Android: no. Manifest protocol_handlers: Chromium desktop 96 for installed apps.
items.gotchas: Custom schemes must be 'web+' plus lowercase ASCII letters. The URL must be https, same-origin, and contain %s. The user approves it (the browser shows a prompt or settings entry). Validate everything that arrives. Combine with launch_handler so a click reuses the open window.

items.title: Payment Request API + Apple Pay / Google Pay
items.what: new PaymentRequest(methods, details).show() opens the browser's native payment sheet: Apple Pay in Safari, Google Pay and saved cards in Chrome. canMakePayment() decides whether to show the wallet button.
items.why: A one-tap Face ID / fingerprint wallet sheet instead of a 16-field card form is the native checkout experience.
items.support: Chrome 60 / Android 53, Edge, Safari 11.1 / iOS 11.3 (Apple Pay method only), Android WebView 136. Firefox: behind a flag only.
items.gotchas: Apple Pay needs domain verification, a merchant ID and a server-side merchant-validation endpoint. Render the platform button (Apple's <apple-pay-button> via its JS SDK, or the -webkit-appearance: -apple-pay-button CSS in Safari) rather than a custom one. Call show() before any await in the click handler. Keep a normal card form with autocomplete=cc-* for Firefox and unsupported cases. Digital goods inside installed store apps follow store rules, not this.

items.title: Credential Management: FedCM, Login Status and Digital Credentials
items.what: navigator.credentials.get with identity providers (FedCM) shows the browser's own account chooser for 'Sign in with X' without redirects, popups or third-party cookies. The digital option (Digital Credentials API) asks the OS wallet for an ID or driver's licence.
items.why: Browser- or OS-drawn account and ID sheets feel like native sign-in. Redirect dances and popup windows feel like the web of 2010.
items.support: FedCM (IdentityCredential): Chrome/Edge 108+; Safari and Firefox no. Login Status API (navigator.login): Chrome 120, Firefox 138. DigitalCredential: Chrome/Edge 141, Safari 26. PasswordCredential: Chromium only.
items.gotchas: FedCM needs the identity provider to implement it (Google Identity Services does). The option shape has evolved (e.g. where the nonce goes), so check the IdP's current docs. Digital Credentials protocols differ by browser (Safari is mdoc-centric; Chrome also supports OpenID4VP), so verify the server request format against the WebKit and Chrome docs. Most apps get 90% of the native feel from correct form markup (autocomplete=username / current-password / new-password) so the OS password manager and passkeys work.

items.title: Contact Picker API
items.what: navigator.contacts.select(['name', 'email', 'tel', 'address', 'icon'], { multiple }) opens the OS contact picker and returns only what the user chose.
items.why: 'Invite from contacts' through the system picker, without uploading the whole address book, is how native apps do invites.
items.support: Chrome Android 80+ and Android WebView. iOS Safari 14.5+ only behind an experimental flag (not shippable). Desktop: none.
items.gotchas: Needs user activation, top-level frame and a secure context. Hide the button when unsupported and fall back to sharing an invite link (Web Share) or typing an address. Treat the returned values as untrusted. Ask only for the properties you need.

items.title: Web Speech: dictation (SpeechRecognition) and text-to-speech (speechSynthesis)
items.what: SpeechRecognition turns speech into text (webkit-prefixed in Safari; unprefixed in Chrome 139 with optional on-device processing). speechSynthesis reads text aloud with OS voices.
items.why: Voice input and read-aloud with system voices make the app feel integrated with the OS's accessibility and voice features.
items.support: SpeechRecognition: Chrome 139 unprefixed (webkit prefix since 33); processLocally, available() and install() for on-device use in Chrome 139 desktop. Safari 14.1 / iOS 14.5 webkit-prefixed. Firefox: Nightly only. speechSynthesis: Chrome 33, Safari 7, Firefox 49 (Android 62); not Android WebView.
items.gotchas: Chrome's default recognition streams audio to Google's servers. Disclose that, or use processLocally where available; this matters for E2E-encrypted apps. Safari needs Siri/Dictation enabled. Voices load asynchronously (voiceschanged) and differ per OS. Long utterances can be cut off in Chrome, so speak sentence by sentence. On phones the keyboard's dictation key is often better UX than your own mic button.

items.title: Screen capture (getDisplayMedia) with CaptureController and contentHint
items.what: getDisplayMedia() lets the user pick a screen, window or tab to share in a call or recording. Chromium extras: CaptureController.setFocusBehavior, selfBrowserSurface, surfaceSwitching and systemAudio options.
items.why: Screen sharing that keeps the user in the call, excludes the call tab itself and is sharp for text matches native Zoom and Teams.
items.support: Desktop: Chrome 72, Edge 79, Firefox 66, Safari 13. Mobile (Chrome Android, iOS/iPadOS Safari, Firefox Android): none. CaptureController and setFocusBehavior: Chrome/Edge 109.
items.gotchas: Hide 'Share screen' on phones (the feature check is enough). Needs user activation; cancelling the picker gives NotAllowedError. Listen for the track's 'ended' event (the browser's own Stop sharing button). setFocusBehavior must be called right after the promise resolves. contentHint 'detail' keeps text sharp; use 'motion' for video. Yurt: no media E2E or browser tests (accepted coverage gap); unit-test the state logic.

items.title: Barcode Detection API (+ Shape/Text detection status)
items.what: BarcodeDetector detects QR codes and barcodes in images or video frames using the OS's native detectors. FaceDetector and TextDetector exist only behind Chromium's experimental flag.
items.why: Instant native QR scanning (join links, invites, pairing) without shipping a 200 KB decoder where the OS can do it.
items.support: Chrome Android 83+ and Android WebView. Chrome desktop on macOS and ChromeOS only (not Windows or Linux). Safari 17+ only behind a flag. Firefox: no. Face/Text detection: experimental flag only; don't ship.
items.gotchas: Always check getSupportedFormats(), because the constructor may exist where detection doesn't work. Run detection at about 10 fps (requestVideoFrameCallback or a timer), not every frame. On iOS the system Camera app already scans QR codes, and a plain <input capture> photo plus decode is a simple fallback. Validate decoded payloads like any input.

items.title: EyeDropper API
items.what: new EyeDropper().open() lets the user pick any pixel on screen and returns an sRGB hex.
items.why: A system-level eyedropper in a color picker is a native design-tool feature.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 95+ desktop (ChromeOS from 120; Linux X11 only, not Wayland). Mobile, Safari, Firefox: none. input.showPicker(): Chrome 99, Safari 16, Firefox 101.
items.gotchas: Needs user activation. Returns sRGB even on wide-gamut displays. <input type=color> is the universal fallback, and on macOS its system panel already includes an eyedropper.

items.title: Idle Detection API (user idle / screen locked)
items.what: IdleDetector reports userState (active or idle) and screenState (locked or unlocked) after a threshold of at least 60 s, with permission.
items.why: Automatic 'away' presence when the user walks off or locks the screen is how Slack and Teams desktop behave.
items.support: Chrome 94+ (desktop and Android), Edge 114+. Safari and Firefox: no (both oppose it on privacy grounds).
items.gotchas: requestPermission needs user activation, so make it an explicit opt-in setting. Privacy-sensitive: never send raw idle timelines to a server. The fallback that works everywhere is Page Visibility plus a 'no input for N minutes' timer (Yurt's presence uses document.hidden).

items.title: Window Management API (multi-screen placement)
items.what: window.getScreenDetails() lists all connected screens with positions and labels. screen.isExtended tells you whether there are several. Windows can be opened, or elements made fullscreen, on a specific screen.
items.why: Presenter views on the laptop with slides on the projector, or trading and dashboard windows per monitor, are native desktop behaviors.
items.support: Chromium 100+ desktop (also exposed on Android, where it's meaningless). Safari and Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: Needs a permission prompt (the name was 'window-placement', now 'window-management') and user activation for popups. screen.isExtended needs no permission, so check it first and don't prompt single-screen users. Listen to 'screenschange' for hot-plugged monitors.

items.title: Web NFC (NDEFReader)
items.what: Read and write NDEF NFC tags (URLs, text, MIME records) from Chrome on Android.
items.why: Tap-a-tag check-ins, inventory and pairing work like a native Android app.
items.support: Chrome Android 89+ and Android WebView. iOS (no Web NFC at all), desktop and Firefox: none.
items.gotchas: Top-level frame, visible page, user activation for the first scan, 'nfc' permission. Scanning pauses when the page is hidden. NDEF only: no payment cards or low-level tag access. Validate URLs read from tags (untrusted).

items.title: Hardware: Web Bluetooth, WebUSB, Web Serial, WebHID
items.what: Device access through browser-mediated choosers: navigator.bluetooth.requestDevice, navigator.usb.requestDevice, navigator.serial.requestPort and navigator.hid.requestDevice, plus getDevices() for previously granted devices.
items.why: Configuring wearables, microcontrollers, 3D printers, game controllers or label printers straight from the app, without a native helper install.
items.support: Web Bluetooth: Chrome desktop (Linux behind a flag) and Android 56. WebUSB: Chrome 61 desktop and Android. Web Serial: Chrome 89 desktop, Chrome Android 148 (138–147 Bluetooth RFCOMM only), Firefox 151 desktop (gated by a generated site-permission add-on, like Web MIDI). WebHID: Chromium 89 desktop. Safari: none of them.
items.gotchas: Every request needs user activation and shows a chooser. Handle 'disconnect' events. Iframes need Permissions-Policy. These are Chromium-centric, so present them as progressive enhancement with a clear 'use Chrome or Edge on desktop' message. Validate all bytes from devices. Avoid them for consumer features that must work on iPhone.

items.title: Compute Pressure API (adapt to CPU/thermal load)
items.what: PressureObserver reports CPU pressure states (nominal, fair, serious, critical) so the app can shed load.
items.why: Native call apps quietly lower resolution or effects when the laptop heats up. Fans spinning and dropped frames make a web app feel heavy.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 125+ desktop. Chrome Android, Safari, Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: Check PressureObserver.knownSources and catch NotSupportedError from observe(). Add hysteresis so quality doesn't flap. Disconnect when the call or heavy view ends.

items.title: Local Font Access (queryLocalFonts)
items.what: window.queryLocalFonts() lists installed fonts (family, fullName, postscriptName), with blob() access to the font data.
items.why: Design and doc tools that show the user's own installed fonts behave like desktop apps.
items.support: Chromium 103+ desktop. Mobile, Safari, Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: Needs a permission prompt and user activation. It's a fingerprinting surface, so only ask in apps where fonts are the feature. Fallback: let users type a family name and render it via CSS local().

items.title: Keyboard Lock and Keyboard Map
items.what: navigator.keyboard.lock(codes) captures system-reserved keys (Esc, Alt+Tab-like shortcuts) while fullscreen. navigator.keyboard.getLayoutMap() maps physical key codes to the user's layout labels.
items.why: Games, remote desktops and VDI get native-like key capture. Shortcut hints showing the right letter on AZERTY or QWERTZ look polished.
items.support: Chromium desktop 68/69 (exposed on Android but not useful). Safari and Firefox: no.
items.gotchas: The lock only applies while the page is fullscreen through requestFullscreen (not F11). If you lock Escape, users must press and hold Esc to exit, so tell them. For ordinary apps, use KeyboardEvent.code for shortcuts and getLayoutMap only for labels.

items.title: Storage Access API (for apps embedded as third-party iframes)
items.what: document.hasStorageAccess() and document.requestStorageAccess() let your iframe, embedded on another site, ask for its first-party cookies and storage after a user gesture.
items.why: Embedded widgets (comments, chat bubbles, docs embeds) that stay signed in, instead of showing 'please log in' or opening popups, feel integrated.
items.support: Safari 11.1 / iOS 11.3, Firefox 65, Edge 85, Chrome 119 desktop / 120 Android. Android WebView: hasStorageAccess only.
items.gotchas: Only relevant if the app is embeddable. Needs user activation. Safari typically requires that the user has used your site first-party before. Storage stays partitioned without the grant. The iframe needs sandbox allow-storage-access-by-user-activation if sandboxed.
